title: What JWTs are
idea: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a signed string of claims, facts such as the user's `_id`. Anyone can read it; only the secret's holder can sign it.
points: A JWT is three base64url strings joined by dots: header, payload and signature.
The payload holds claims. `iat` (issued at) and `exp` (expiry) are standard names.
Base64url is an encoding, not encryption, so never put secrets in the payload.
`jwt.verify` recomputes the signature and rejects edited or expired tokens.

steps.caption: A token is three base64url parts joined by dots: header, payload and signature.
Decoding needs no key. The header names the algorithm; the payload shows `_id`, `username`, `iat` and `exp`.
The signature is a fingerprint of the first two parts, made with the server's secret.
Change `_id` to another user's id and the old signature no longer fits, so `jwt.verify` throws.
Signing the edited payload needs the secret. Without it, nobody can forge a token the server accepts.

code.title: Sign, read, verify
code.caption: Anyone can decode the header and payload with `Buffer`; no secret needed. `exp - iat` is the lifetime in seconds.

pitfalls: Never put passwords or private data in a payload; base64url is encoding, not encryption.
`jwt.decode` reads claims without checking the signature. Use `jwt.verify` before you trust a token.
Use a long, random secret from `.env`; a short one can be guessed offline.

quiz.why: The payload is only encoded, so anyone can read `u-101`. The secret is used to sign and never appears in the token.

takeaway: Anyone can read a JWT; only the secret's holder can change it.
